tier_reason: Third-party (Wuffs authors) mimic benchmark against libpng 1.6.37 with public code (google/wuffs script/bench-rust-png/src/main.rs for the Rust side, test/c/std/png.c plus test/c/mimiclib/png.c for libpng, built with -O3), stated toolchains (Rust 1.48 cargo --release, gcc 10.2.1 / clang 11.0.1, Debian Bullseye) and CPU (Intel Core i5-10210U); all five rust_png rows match the record.

corrections.workload: PNG decode to BGRA in the Wuffs 'mimic' benchmarks on five test images (bricks-gray 19k 8bpp, hat 40k 24bpp, bricks-dither 77k 8bpp, hibiscus.primitive 552k 32bpp with checksum verification, harvesters 4002k 24bpp), Rust 1.48 with png 0.17.5 / deflate 1.0.0 / miniz_oxide 0.5.3 vs Debian's libpng 1.6.37 through its simplified API; 5 reps after a warm-up rep.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Wuffs doc/benchmarks.md (September 2022), rust_png decode vs mimiclibpng: 19k_8bpp 187 vs 122 MB/s (1.53x), 40k_24bpp 260 vs 147 MB/s (1.77x), 77k_8bpp 330 vs 370 MB/s (0.89x), 552k_32bpp_verify_checksum 299 vs 289 MB/s (1.03x), 4002k_24bpp 264 vs 214 MB/s (1.23x); ratios are the page's vs_mimic column. Faster than libpng on four of five images. Crate README: 'Performance is typically on par with or better than libpng' and an fdeflate-powered fast encoding mode 'dramatically faster than the fastest mode of libpng while simultaneously providing better compression ratio' (no numbers on that page).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust side: Rust 1.48, `cargo run --release` in script/bench-rust-png (default release profile, no profile overrides in its Cargo.toml), png 0.17.5. libpng side: Debian Bullseye's packaged libpng 1.6.37 linked into the Wuffs C harness test/c/std/png.c, compiled with gcc 10.2.1 or clang 11.0.1 at -O3 plus '-DWUFFS_MIMIC -lm -lpng -lz' (per the comment at the top of png.c); Debian's own build flags for libpng are not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 522 stars; png crate has 244.8 million crates.io downloads (79.8 million recent)
corrections.caveats: Rust crate, not C++: it fails the C++ language filter and is usable from C++ only through FFI. Mixed result: one of five images is slower than libpng (0.89x on 77k_8bpp). The numbers are for png 0.17.5 measured in September 2022 on one laptop CPU; the current release is 0.18.1 (rust-version 1.81, fdeflate-based decoding) and has not been re-measured on that page. The same page shows Wuffs' own C decoder at 1.55x-3.16x of libpng, faster than rust_png on every image. The Rust harness times an extra RGB/RGBA-to-BGRA conversion loop that libpng's simplified API does internally. The crate's own benches/decoder.rs is a criterion self-benchmark with no libpng comparison. The fast-encode claim has no numbers on the crate page. zune-image's benchmarks/benchmark-results.md (Darwin, CPU not named) compares against the spng binding, not libpng: image-rs/png is faster than spng on all four PNG decode cases (for example 149.3 ms vs 297.4 ms on the baseline image) but slower than zune-png on two of them.

notes: Numbers verified line by line in the Wuffs doc; the record said six images but the rust_png benchmark has five (552k appears once). Language field is correctly Rust; orchestrator should apply the C++ language-filter policy (keep with shortcoming or move to an 'any language' bucket). Metadata checked on github.com: MIT OR Apache-2.0, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-23.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed HiPC 2021 paper that names libjpeg-turbo and nvJPEG as baselines, but every host carrying it (arXiv, ar5iv, ADS, hgpu.org, encode.su, Uni Mainz, Hugging Face, OpenAlex) is egress-blocked, so the numbers are snippet-only and no code exists; per the orchestrator's rule it stays a reference record at C.

corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the paper could not be opened (arXiv, ar5iv, ADS, hgpu.org, encode.su, the Mainz HPC group page, Hugging Face and OpenAlex are all blocked here); benchmark_url is the arXiv PDF URL as it appears in search results, not opened. Its existence and venue are corroborated by several independent search results, including the GPULZ paper's reference list: 'André Weißenberger and Bertil Schmidt. Accelerating jpeg decompression on gpus. 2021 IEEE 28th International Conference on High Performance Computing, Data, and Analytics (HiPC), pages 121-130.' My own search snippets show only the A100 figures (up to 51x over libjpeg-turbo, 8.0x over nvJPEG); the V100 figures (34x, 5.7x) and the 3.4x over nvJPEG's A100 hardware decoder come from the search agent's snippet. Unknown: CPU model and thread count for libjpeg-turbo (a single-threaded CPU baseline would inflate the 51x), CUDA and nvJPEG versions, image set, and whether host-device transfers are timed. No code: the author's GitHub account (weissenberger) has exactly four repositories (HIPSW4, bzip2gpu, multians, gpuhd), none a JPEG decoder.

notes: Real paper, real named baselines, no code and no openable source in this environment; kept as reference at C. A retier needs an environment that reaches arXiv or IEEE to read the setup section.

tier_reason: Author-run shootout of the author's own codec with a public driver (RunBenchmark.py) and stated CPU (i7-12700H), but the measured fNBLI.exe is a prebuilt binary with no stated compiler or flags, so it falls short of A; first-party, so C.

corrections.baseline: PNG encoded and decoded through Pillow 10.1.0's own PNG codec (PngImagePlugin over Pillow's zlib-based 'zip' codec, not libpng), optipng 0.7.7 for optimized PNG encoding, and libwebp lossless via Pillow 10.1.0
corrections.claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark README, CLIC2021 totals (585 images, 4.1 GB, single-threaded): fNBLI 43.164 s compress, 27.450 s decompress, 1,337,587,020 bytes; Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes; PNG optipng -o2 4395.069 s, 26.625 s, 1,905,215,734 bytes; Pillow WebP lossless m5 1112.134 s, 49.442 s, 1,475,908,700 bytes. That is 7.8x faster encode and 1.23x faster decode than Pillow PNG with 33% smaller files, and 25.8x faster encode and 1.80x faster decode than WebP lossless m5 with 9% smaller files (derived from page data); decoding is slightly slower than optipng-optimized PNG (27.450 s vs 26.625 s at -o2 and 25.799 s at -o5). NBLI README restates these as fNBLI 94.8 MB/s compress and 149.1 MB/s decompress, 29.79% smaller than optipng PNG, vs PNG 12.2 / 121.5 MB/s and WebP -5 3.7 / 82.8 MB/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt fNBLI.exe v0.4 (banner 'v0.4, 202409', needs AVX2); compiler and flags for that binary are not stated, and the README gives a build command (g++ -O3 -static) only for the NBLI prototype in src/NBLI, not for src/fNBLI. Baselines: Pillow 10.1.0 on Python 3.9, optipng 0.7.7.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded lossless compression and decompression of the CLIC2021 training set (585 RGB 24-bit .pnm images, 4.1 GB) and six other datasets, timed per dataset with file I/O included, in the author's Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout (RunBenchmark.py, which checks the round trip is lossless).
corrections.caveats: Author-run benchmark of the author's own codec. The timing harness is asymmetric: Pillow codecs run in-process through exec(), while fNBLI.exe is launched with os.system once per image, so fNBLI also pays process start-up per file (this handicaps fNBLI, not the baselines). The PNG baseline is Pillow's own zlib-based PNG codec, not libpng. Decoding is not faster than optipng-optimized PNG (27.450 s vs 26.625 s / 25.799 s on CLIC2021). The fNBLI source was published on 2026-07-18 (commit 6561fc8, 2,804 added lines under src/fNBLI including AVX2 and rANS code) and carries the same 'v0.4, 202409' banner as the benchmarked binary, but the binary predates the source, the README still links fNBLI.exe, the shootout's format table still marks fNBLI as not open source, and there is no build recipe for it, so binary-to-source correspondence is unverified. Single benchmark machine (i7-12700H, Windows 10).

notes: The orchestrator's premise that fNBLI is binary-only is out of date: src/fNBLI source exists since 2026-07-18 under the repo's GPL-3.0, so has_code stays true and usability copyable. All shootout numbers and the README MB/s figures check out (94.8 MB/s = 4,091,841,959 bytes / 43.164 s); the record's claim that Pillow pays per-file process overhead was wrong and is corrected. No known correctness bug; the driver verifies losslessness.
